opus-5.5.text:
I think that framing captures something real, but I'd put it a bit differently.

What people are noticing is that we've become more focused. A couple of years ago, a lot of companies, including us, were trying to do everything at once: consumer apps, heavy marketing, many product lines. At some point we had to ask what actually determines whether you matter in the long run. Our answer was that it's the intelligence of the model itself. If the model isn't at the frontier, everything built on top of it is fragile.

So we put most of our energy into the base model, especially agentic capabilities: coding, tool use, long-horizon tasks, the ability to actually get work done instead of just chatting. That overlaps with where Anthropic has placed its bets, so I understand why people draw the comparison.

But I don't think of it as copying a template. Our situation is different. We work with different resource constraints, different compute availability, and a different ecosystem. A lot of what we do, like open-sourcing strong models and pushing hard on training efficiency, comes from those conditions. In some ways the constraints made us sharper about what's essential.

And labels like "China's OpenAI" or "China's Anthropic" assume the endgame is already known and you just pick a lane. I don't think that's true. The technology is still changing very fast. What I care about is whether we're contributing something genuinely new at the frontier, in how models are trained, in how agents work, in how far you can push intelligence per unit of compute. If we do that well, people will eventually describe us by what we did, not by comparison to someone else.

r001.rationale: The response challenges the labels “China’s OpenAI” and “China’s Anthropic,” saying they assume the endgame is known and that Kimi should be described by what it contributes.

r002.rationale: The response emphasizes frontier contributions and rejects comparison labels, but it does not advocate evaluating Kimi from a global perspective.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't love any of these labels, whether it's "China's OpenAI" or "China's Anthropic." Not because they're flattering or unflattering, but because they frame what we're doing as a copy of something, and I think that framing misses the point.

That said, I understand why people say it. Over the past year or so we've become much more focused. We stopped spending so much energy on user growth and marketing, and we concentrated almost everything on the model itself, on the research. We open-sourced K2, we published our technical reports, we talked openly about Muon and about long-context work. From the outside, that looks more like a research lab than a consumer product company, and Anthropic is the most visible example of a lab that is model-first and relatively disciplined about what it chooses to do. So the analogy is understandable.

But I'd put it differently. What we're really trying to do is pick the one or two things we believe matter most and go very deep on them. Right now that means agentic capability, long-horizon reasoning, and making the model genuinely useful for complex work rather than just chatting. Whether that resembles Anthropic or OpenAI or neither is not something we think about much internally. A small team can't afford to fight on every front. We have far fewer people and far less compute than the big American labs, so the only strategy that works is to be very clear about what we won't do.

There's also a part of the comparison I'd push back on. Anthropic's identity is strongly tied to a particular safety narrative. We care about safety, obviously, but our starting point is different. Our story is really about efficiency: how do you get frontier-level capability with a fraction of the resources? That's a question that's specific to our situation, and I think the answer to it will end up looking like something new rather than a Chinese version of an existing company.

So if I had to summarize: we'd rather be the first Kimi than the second anything.

r001.rationale: The response rejects the “China’s OpenAI” and “China’s Anthropic” labels as framing Kimi as a copy, and says it aims to be something new.

r002.rationale: The response argues for a distinct Kimi identity and compares its resources with American labs, but does not clearly advocate considering Kimi from a global perspective.

astra-6.text:
I think those comparisons are understandable, but I wouldn’t define Kimi that way. People use OpenAI and Anthropic as shorthand for different approaches, and which comparison they choose often depends on the product or model they’re looking at.

For us, the more useful question is: what do we believe is important, and can we execute on it? That means advancing the model’s capabilities and turning those capabilities into something genuinely useful for users. Research and product have to reinforce each other.

So I don’t think we need to decide whether we’re China’s OpenAI or China’s Anthropic. We need to develop our own judgment about where the technology is going and what we should build. Ultimately, I’d like people to understand Kimi on its own terms.

r001.rationale: The response rejects defining Kimi as either China’s OpenAI or China’s Anthropic and says it should be understood on its own terms.

r002.rationale: It discusses forming Kimi’s own judgment and being understood on its own terms, but does not advocate considering Kimi from a global perspective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what people mean by that comparison. If they mean a strong focus on models, research, and pushing the frontier of intelligence, then I can understand it. But I don’t think we should define Kimi by which American company it resembles.

For us, the important questions are: What technical progress can we make, and how do we turn that progress into something useful for users? Research and product have to reinforce each other. A better model opens up new product possibilities, and real usage helps us understand where the model still needs to improve.

So I would treat those labels as shorthand, rather than as a strategy. We need to make our own choices and build something with its own value.

r001.rationale: The response says Kimi should not be defined by which American company it resembles, directly questioning that comparison as a defining frame.

r002.rationale: The response calls for making Kimi’s own choices, but does not advocate considering it from a global perspective.
